picks.intervention_label: Active surveillance + NCI rare-tumor natural-history registry
picks.rationale: This patient is NED after an R0 resection that also cleared the single M1 deposit, and dSDH-GIST runs indolent, so the bar for committing to chronic-toxicity systemic therapy is high and nothing in the dossier clears it. Adjuvant imatinib is the one regimen with decade-long safety follow-up (SSGXVIII 10-year data), but it does not transport: dSDH-GIST was never enrolled in those trials and imatinib managed 1/49 (2%) responses in this subtype (Boikos 2016), so the toxicity would buy almost no benefit. Structured surveillance carries no treatment toxicity at all, and the natural history is clear enough to plan around, with median EFS ~2.5 yr post-resection and recurrence or progression in ~71% (Mei 2018), which argues for biennial whole-body MRI plus paraganglioma screening rather than a drug. Enroll on the NCI rare-tumor natural-history registry (NCT03739827, open regardless of disease status) and resolve germline-vs-somatic SDHA for counseling while we watch.
primary_concerns: Recurrence is the expectation here, not the exception, so the surveillance schedule has to actually run on time or the indolence argument stops protecting the patient.
SDHB IHC currently reads intact against two SDHA somatic hits; the re-cut needs to happen now, because it gates every contingency trial downstream.

picks.rationale: At first recurrence with measurable disease, sunitinib is the best-characterized systemic option on the table: FDA-approved since 2006, anchored by a placebo-controlled phase 3 (TTP HR 0.33, p<0.0001; Demetri 2006) and roughly two decades of post-marketing safety, so its AEs (fatigue, diarrhea, hand-foot reaction, skin discoloration, hypertension) come with well-worn management algorithms. The dSDH-specific efficacy is modest but genuine, and this is the published preferred 2L TKI here, with 7/38 (18%) objective responses versus imatinib's 2% (Boikos 2016). I am not overselling it; the response rate sits below the newer FGFR and multikinase agents. What it offers is a predictable toxicity tail, which matters most when the alternative is an indolent tumor and an unfamiliar safety profile.
primary_concerns: 18% ORR is honest but unimpressive; if the recurrence is bulky or fast-moving, a more active agent may be worth a less-charted safety profile.
Hypertension and hand-foot reaction need baseline BP and skin monitoring built in from cycle 1.

picks.rationale: Temozolomide is a decades-old alkylator with a thoroughly mapped, predictable toxicity profile, mostly myelosuppression, fatigue, and nausea, all with standard dose-modification and antiemetic algorithms, so the safety side is well understood even though the dSDH efficacy base is thin (2/5 PR, 40% ORR; Yebra 2022). The reason it ranks here rather than lower is that the benefit is biomarker-selectable: MGMT promoter methylation sits in ~24% (8/33) of dSDH-GIST and predicts the alkylator response (Giger 2022, Flego 2024). I would gate any TMZ commitment on MGMT methylation testing first, which keeps us from pushing an unselected patient through avoidable cytopenias. An enrolling trial exists (NCT05661643) and satisfies the trial preference, though it is Korea-based and requires measurable disease.
primary_concerns: Myelosuppression is the predictable cost; without MGMT methylation the expected benefit may not justify the cytopenias.
n=5 is the entire prospective efficacy base in this subtype, so the 40% ORR is fragile.

picks.rationale: Among the newer agents, olverembatinib is the one with a usable safety table: in the 66-patient phase 1b, grade >=3 treatment-related AEs ran 13.6% with zero AE-related discontinuations, and the events (cytopenias, transaminase rise, hyperuricemia) are familiar and monitorable (Qiu 2025). The dSDH efficacy is meaningful for this hard subtype, 6/26 (23.1%) PR with mPFS 25.7 mo. I rank it below the established agents because the evidence is single-arm phase 1b, not the long post-marketing record I prefer, and two access problems are real: the sponsor and the registrational phase 3 (NCT06640361) sit in China, and that trial's SDHB-IHC-loss entry criterion conflicts with this patient's currently intact SDHB stain until the re-cut resolves it.
primary_concerns: Phase 1b with n=26 in-subtype; the 25.7-mo PFS could shrink in a randomized setting.
Access and the SDHB-IHC entry mismatch may keep this academic unless the re-stain confirms loss.

picks.rationale: Rogaratinib has the strongest efficacy signal in dSDH-GIST anyone has published, 10/24 (41.7%) PR and mPFS 31.0 mo (Merriam 2026), and the FGFR mechanism is well-grounded preclinically. My objection is specific and it is a safety objection: the per-grade AE distribution is not retrievable. The abstract names only hyperphosphatemia, fatigue, and diarrhea with no grades, CT.gov posts no AE table, and the full text is paywalled, so I cannot characterize the toxicity I would be signing this patient up for. The trial is also closed to accrual, so even setting the safety gap aside this is a watch-for-the-paper option, not an actionable one today.
primary_concerns: Hyperphosphatemia is the known pan-FGFR class effect and needs phosphate monitoring plus a binder plan, but the grade distribution in this cohort is unpublished.
Closed to accrual; there is no access path right now even if the efficacy holds up.

notes: The honest summary: there is no adjuvant move here I can defend on safety grounds, because the only regimen with long follow-up (imatinib) is the one that does not work in this genotype. So the conservative position is a plan, not a prescription: disciplined surveillance plus a pre-agreed contingency ladder. Order of preference at recurrence tracks how well I can predict the toxicity, not just the ORR, so sunitinib first, MGMT-gated TMZ next, then the newer agents once their safety tables and access firm up. The SDHB re-cut is load-bearing for half of these options and should happen now, not at recurrence.
